Queen of the Ring

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 10:56
Instaread

QUEEN OF THE RING is such a well-meaning movie that I didn’t mind it that much even though it’s quite bad. It’s a biopic of pioneering women’s wrestler Millie Burke, based on the 2010 book The Queen of the Ring: Sex, Muscles, Diamonds, and the Making of an American Legend by Jeff Leen. That’s a whole lot of research right there, but the adaptation by writer/director Ash Avildsen (AMERICAN SATAN) plays like a torn from the headlines TV quickie trying to summarize the basics. The whole feeling of it reminds me of the trailers I’ve seen for Angel Studios biopics of Jimmy Stewart and whatsisname Hershey, or of one of the Hallmark movies where they get ambitious and make it period even though it’s kinda beyond their means.

Mildred “Millie” Bliss (Emily Bett Rickards, BROOKLYN) is a single mother who enjoys having muscular arms but is disillusioned about other aspects of her life, such as working as a waitress at the diner owned by her mother (Cara Buono, KICKING AND SCREAMING). So when she goes to a (men’s) wrestling match in town and learns some basic lingo from a guy in the crowd (Tyler Posey, Teen Wolf) she stands wide-eyed and declares, “This is my destiny.”

The guy from the match, G. Bill, shows up in the diner with his dad Billy Wolfe (Josh Lucas, STEALTH), the heel wrestler she saw angering the crowd, and she begs him to train her to wrestle. Eventually he agrees to a try out against a man just to get rid of her, but is blown away when she wins with an armlock. (It doesn’t seem that impressive from here.)

The movie makes a big deal about women’s wrestling (they prefer “lady wrestling”) being illegal, so I kept expecting some police trouble like in STRAIGHT OUTTA COMPTON, but I guess I misunderstood. It’s illegal in some states, so they don’t go to those. They travel carnivals via montages set to modern country-ish rock (there are five songs by the band Larkin Poe and four by the singer Des Rocs). Millie pretends to take on challengers from the crowd, inspiring little girls like Meryl Streep in THE POST. There’s drama built around trying to get bigger gigs and competition with other promotions, leading to shoots (real fights).

I guess the last two things I’ve seen Lucas in were FORD V FERRARI (2019) and J. EDGAR (2011), so it was kind of cool to see him back as an older man, with a cauliflower ear and an old-timey physique. During training Billy and Millie do some sexy moves, fall in love, they get married and he’s her manager. It’s romantic until she catches him cheating, then when he hits her. She leaves him for a while but has trouble booking herself and reluctantly reunites for a business relationship that turns into a business marriage. The whole time G. Bill clearly loves her, so there’s tension there.

This whole time people keep not believing she can wrestle and be a single mother, then congratulating her when she does, but we mostly don’t see the kid Joe Jr. until he’s grown. There’s a CONAN THE BARBARIAN aging scene where she’s riding a carousel and as it rotates he switches from toddler (Izzy Avildsen) to kid (Greyson Neumann). Later he’s an adult played by Gavin Casalegno (“Young Shem,” NOAH) and wants to help her career.

The most fun part is the friendships (and sometimes rivalries) with other wrestlers including Elvira Snodgrass (Marie Avgeropoulos, HUNT TO KILL, JIU JITSU), and Mae Young (Francesca Eastwood). We don’t see Mae wrestle enough, but Eastwood was so good in M.F.A. and has such striking features, I liked seeing her as the loyal best friend. Deborah Ann Woll (THE CYCLE) shows up later as Gladys “Killem” Gillem, and is great in her scenes (including the wrestling), so I wish it was a bigger role.

After seeing Jackie Robinson on TV Billy recruits a trio of Black women wrestlers, Babs Wingo (Damaris Lewis, BLACKKKLANSMAN), Marva Scott (Cameren Jackson, THEY DEVOUR) and Ethel Johnson (WWE’s Trinity McCray Fatu). If I had to guess I’d say some of these white wrestlers had a problem with it, but here they’re all on the same page. “Together, we gotta shake things up and break walls down in this country.” We do see them experience racism when a hotel doesn’t want to give them rooms so Millie buys the place out. Good for her using rich lady privilege to help her friends, bad for her rewarding the hotel for being racist. The movie seemed to believe the man had been stuck it to, but I disagreed.

Millie also has a lightly sketched friendship with a male wrestler who takes something she said as inspiration to reinvent himself as Gorgeous George (Adam Demos, SPA WEEKEND), a wrestler famous enough that I remember my dad telling me about him when I was a kid (comparing him to WWF’s “Adorable” Adrian Adonis). I was happy to see Martin Kove (STEEL JUSTICE) and Walton Goggins (THE NEXT KARATE KID) show up as promoters Al Haft and Jack Pfefer, but neither is a role worthy of their talents.

There’s at least as much awkwardly explaining stuff through dialogue as you’d expect. But thankfully the only really painful Mike-Meyers-in-BOHEMIAN-RHAPSODY moment is the scene where Vince McMahon Sr. (director cameo) mentions that his son Vince Jr. disapproves of promoters being part of the storyline. You see because later Jr. would be the CEO of WWF and make his whole family the center of the storyline. Just a little good-natured ribbing about the ego of a man who has separate Wikipedia pages for “Vince McMahon sexual misconduct allegations” and “Vince McMahon sex trafficking scandal.”

Speaking of terrible people, there’s also a historical figure cameo from outside of the wrestling world when Millie is at a party and gets to defend lady wrestling from Senator Joseph McCarthy (Barron Boedecker)’s wife Jean (Abi Van Andel, THE ALTO KNIGHTS). That’s probly a FORREST GUMP/BLUE MOONism but we don’t get enough on the interesting topic of “people thought it was obscene for women to wrestle,” so I’ll take it.

I couldn’t help but compare this to CHRISTY, last year’s biopic of women’s boxing pioneer Christy Martin. It’s a different sport and time period, but overlaps in that it’s a true story about a woman convincing a sexist trainer to give her a chance and having a marriage of convenience with him that becomes (in that case much more) abusive while being the face of a growing women’s sport and challenging notions about gender. But CHRISTY is simply a far better movie on every possible front – better filmmaking and performances, more natural, more layered, more emotional.

At least that seems as plain as day to me, but QUEEN OF THE RING has a higher rating on Metacritic. I suppose it feels more like the underdog since it’s struggling to even feel like a real movie. I don’t know how small the budget it is, but the feeling is cheap. There’s a production value that couldn’t be accomplished on a shoe-string – carnival sets, crowds, costumes. Plenty of polos, suspenders and hats, let me tell you. But it looks very clean and artificial and it all feels like playing dress up. About halfway through there’s a montage done in black and white where they amp up the old-timey-ness…


…and it made me sad the rest of the movie wasn’t like that. That would’ve worked better.

Most of the time they’re working real hard to talk old timey, then in one scene Millie says, “Oh, you gotta be shittin me.” Which you may also find yourself saying throughout.

I’m of two minds about Rickards as Millie. On one hand with her accent and spunky dialogue she kinda comes across like dollar store Margaret Qualley. On the other hand she’s doing what she can with a screenplay seemingly typed directly onto the nose, and as far as the physical part of the role – the biceps, the wrestling moves – she’s clearly very dedicated. I kinda liked her, if more in theory than in practice.

According to Wikipedia, writer/director Avildsen is a former software pirate, a metalcore vocalist in a band called Reflux, and yes, as I assumed, the son of Oscar-winning ROCKY and THE KARATE KID director John G. Avildsen. So he’s a (reportedly estranged) nepo-baby directing Clint Eastwood’s daughter and, in one scene, Nicolas Cage’s son Weston, and he’s made one of the central characters the son of a famous wrestler. I wonder if he felt weird having that character be in love with his dad’s wife? I think I would feel self conscious about that.

It does turn out to come from the real story, though. After a movie like this it’s fun to read up on it a little and see how close it comes to being kinda true. There’s definitely lots of fudging the timeline, but at least they stuck to a group of wrestlers who really did come up together and broke some new ground (though who knows, the way all wrestlers self-mythologize). I do get the sense they whitewashed Billy Wolfe a little, making him a well-meaning fuckup rather than a sleazy sex-harassing exploiter. But I do think the way it’s portrayed in the movie, with the wrestlers understanding some of his flaws but also liking some things about working with him, is pretty interesting.

The only wrestler portrayed in QUEEN OF THE RING I remember being around when I watched wrestling as a kid was the Fabulous Moolah. I didn’t know it was supposed to be her, but I guess the wrestler Mickie James plays her as one of the next generation of wrestlers Millie is training. The real Fabulous Moolah was on the Hulk Hogan’s Rock ’n Wrestling cartoon and later in the documentary LIPSTICK AND DYNAMITE (along with the wrestlers played here by Woll and Eastwood). But reading up on her I see that after she died she was accused of pimping out and otherwise exploiting her proteges. Maybe that’s why they didn’t seem to like her in the documentary

In that review more than 20 years ago I wrote, “I kept thinking this would make a real good non-documentary. A period epic about the time period they’re talking about. It’s usually a bad idea to re-enact a documentary with actors, but here would be a way to see these great stories and this world they’re talking about playing out around you like you’re really there, instead of hearing it told as a story decades later.”

So I guess I sort of got my wish. My new wish is for someone to do a much better job at my first wish. Thank you for your consideration in this matter.
